title: From Consent to Rehab: Orthopedic Language Access
summary: Protect LEP patients through orthopedic surgery with interpreted consent, discharge teach-back, rehab access, and quality metrics. (October 2026)
body_markdown:
###


Record the language and dialect, the interpreter or AI session identifier, the mode, duration, participants, questions asked, and teach-back outcomes. Attach written materials in the patient's preferred language and apply quality controls to fasting rules, anticoagulant timing, and implant information before the form is signed.


###


Walk through medications, wound care, warning signs, and weight-bearing limits with an interpreter present, then ask the patient to restate the plan and show any required movements or device use. Correct gaps on the spot and note the result in the chart so the next clinician knows what was confirmed.


###


Offer professional interpretation first and document that the offer was made. If the patient still prefers a family member for a non-clinical conversation, that choice can be honored, but weight-bearing instructions, consent, and medication counseling should still include a qualified interpreter because a relative may soften bad news or miss technical terms.


###


Any instruction describing weight bearing as tolerated versus non-weight bearing, along with device use for crutches or walkers, needs interpreted teach-back and a physical demonstration. Patients should show the load and not merely repeat the phrase, since a misunderstood term can overload a fixation or graft.


###


Track interpretation start times, consent and discharge teach-back completion, rehab attendance, and communication incidents tied to misunderstanding or delay, broken out by language and care stage. Review these monthly with a cross-functional workgroup so gaps in handoffs or templates get corrected quickly.
